title: De insigni paradoxo, quod in analysi maximorum et minimorum occurrit

deep.reconstruction: Context (§§1–15): Euler minimizes the 'momentum' ∫√x ds. This is Maupertuis' action for a heavy body whose speed is ∝√x, where x is the depth below the horizontal line on which the speed vanishes. The Euler–Lagrange equation is ∂.(p√x/√(1+pp)) = 0, with p = dy/dx. Its first integral p√x/√(1+p²) = C gives parabolic trajectories. Between F and H (depths f and h, horizontal separation essentially g) there are two parabolas if gg < fh, one if gg = fh, and none (imaginary) if gg > fh. The case gg = fh is the 'longest throw': H lies on the envelope (the parabola of safety). There the action is ⅔(f+h)^{3/2}. Yet the broken path F→f→h→H has action ⅔(f^{3/2}+h^{3/2}): straight down to the line x=0, along it, and straight up. That is always smaller. This is the paradox. On this page Euler finishes the explanation begun in §15. On the verticals Ff and hH we have dy=0, so p=0 and the expression vanishes. On the horizontal fh we have x=0, so it 'again vanishes'. Hence the broken path satisfies the first integral with C=0 piecewise and is 'contained in the calculus', though it is not one continuous analytic curve. He then gives an analogy. A curve can have several local minima of its ordinates, very different in size, each smaller than its neighbours on either side. Likewise, when the calculus yields two parabolas between F and H, both actions can be minima (local, 'in suo genere') even though they differ greatly. In modern terms this is the distinction between local and global extrema, applied to a functional. It is used to reconcile two stationary curves with each other and with a lower-valued nonsmooth competitor.
errors: Euler's claim that, when two parabolas join F and H, the action may be minimal for both is not correct by later sufficiency theory (Jacobi). Only the arc that does not touch the envelope (parabola of safety) between F and H is free of a conjugate (kinetic-focal) point. The other arc touches the envelope before reaching H, so it is not even a weak local minimum (it is a saddle). The local-minima-of-a-function analogy fails here: of the two extremals, only one can be a local minimum.

Minor point: the broken path lies on the degenerate line x=0, where the integrand (the 'Jacobi metric' √x ds) vanishes. Its legitimacy as a limit of admissible curves (e.g. a horizontal run at depth ε→0) is implicit rather than argued.

ideas.what: Discontinuous (broken) extremal along the degenerate boundary line x=0, satisfying the first integral with constant 0 piecewise, and beating the smooth extremal
ideas.modern_name: Goldschmidt-type discontinuous solution / broken extremal on a degenerate boundary of a Jacobi metric
ideas.usually_credited_to: B. Goldschmidt (1831) for the minimal surface of revolution; Weierstrass–Erdmann theory of broken extremals later
ideas.where_published: E735 itself (posthumous, Mémoires de l'Acad. St-Pétersbourg T. III, 1811)

ideas.what: Distinguishing local ('in suo genere') minima from the true minimum of a functional, by analogy with several local minima of the ordinates of one curve
ideas.modern_name: local vs global minimum in the calculus of variations
ideas.usually_credited_to: implicit in Lagrange / Legendre; made rigorous by Weierstrass

ideas.what: Coalescence of the two extremals at gg = fh, identified with the longest throw (envelope)
ideas.modern_name: envelope of extremals / conjugate point (kinetic focus) boundary

missed.claim: Euler's family ∫√x ds is the α=1/2 member of the family ∫x^α ds. That family also contains the minimal surface of revolution (α=1; catenary vs Goldschmidt solution) and the brachistochrone (α=−1/2). Euler already exhibits the full Goldschmidt phenomenon here, 20 years before Goldschmidt: two extremals, then one, then none; a broken solution along the axis; and that broken solution beating the smooth one. He also shows the broken solution fits the Euler–Lagrange first integral with constant 0. The parallel is rarely, if ever, drawn in the history of discontinuous solutions.
missed.quote: at vero pro via horizontali fh, propter x = 0, iterum evanescit
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It would credit Euler with an early Goldschmidt-type analysis and situate E735 in the prehistory of broken extremals and degenerate (Jacobi-metric) boundaries.

missed.claim: Euler leaves open which of the two parabolas is a genuine minimum. He asserts both may be. The question is settled by Jacobi's conjugate-point theory: only the arc not reaching the envelope qualifies. His remark that the two-extremal and coalescing cases are tied to the 'longest throw' envelope points straight at the conjugate-point criterion, but he does not draw that conclusion.
missed.quote: momenta pro utraque minima esse posse, etiamsi a se invicem plurimum differant
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historically clean precursor example of the conjugate-point phenomenon, useful for teaching and for history of sufficiency conditions.

deep.surprise_reason: The page closes a known posthumous paper on a variational paradox. Its content, a discontinuous solution satisfying the first integral and local-vs-global minima, anticipates Goldschmidt and Jacobi. However, the paper is catalogued, and some historians (possibly Goldstine) may already discuss it. The final claim is also partly wrong.
